\begin{document}

\title{Compact beam-ionized plasma neutralizer for high-current compact-cyclotron
axial injection: design constraints and simulation framework}

\author{Chong Shik Park}
\email{kuphy@korea.ac.kr}
\affiliation{Department of Accelerator Science and Center for Accelerator Research,
Korea University, Sejong, 30019 Republic of Korea}

\date{\today}

\begin{abstract}
High-current compact cyclotrons require multi-mA, low-energy proton beams to be
transported through a short axial injection line whose space-charge forces are
largely uncompensated. We study a compact gas cell, placed between the RF buncher and
the main solenoid, in which the beam ionizes $\Htwo$ or Kr to build a compensating
electron column. For a \numEkev~keV, \numIavgma~mA proton beam of \numabeammm~mm radius
the generalized perveance is $K_0=\numKzero$, and a laminar beam expands by a factor
\numgrowthKzero{} over the \numLcellcm-cm cell length. Using Rudd-model ionization
cross sections we obtain neutralization build-up times of \numtauHtwous~$\mu$s for
$\Htwo$ at $\numpHtwo$~Torr and \numtauKrus~$\mu$s for Kr at $\numpKr$~Torr; Kr reaches
the $\Htwo$ build-up rate at $\numpKrequal$~Torr, not at a tenfold lower pressure.
A time-scale analysis shows that the achievable neutralization is set by electron
confinement rather than by the ionization rate: freely escaping secondary electrons
limit cell-local neutralization to $\eta\sim10^{-3}$, and for a bunched beam
(\numfRFmhz~MHz, bunching factor $B_f$) electrons cross the beam in
\numtcrossns~ns whereas the inter-bunch gap lasts \numgapns~ns, so an axial magnetic
field of order \numBconfine~mT or electrostatic end plugs are required. Even with an
ideal static background, peak-bunch perveance is reduced only to
$\Keff/K_0\approx1-\etaavg/B_f$ (\numKeffpeakstatic{} for $\etaavg=0.9$, $B_f=\numBf$).
Three-dimensional electrostatic WarpX simulations of a DC beam in a seeded plasma column
with a 0.15~T cell solenoid show that the outcome over the first \numpicns~ns is set by
ion expulsion. At $\numpHtwo$~Torr $\Htwo$ the beam-core net neutralization reaches
\numpicHtwoeta{} ($\Keff/K_0=\numpicHtwokeff$) because $\Htwo^+$ ions leave the core, whereas
for Kr it stays at \numpicKretamin--\numpicKretamax{} at all pressures because the heavy
Kr$^+$ ions remain. These results start from a prescribed plasma and do not model the
build-up itself. Electrostatic end plugs at least 10~mm wide with the cell solenoid hold the
electrons for \numstCWtauc~$\mu$s on the production grid, keeping \numstCWeta{} core
compensation; narrow plugs shorten the confinement and degrade the beam. Envelope and particle
tracking to the spiral inflector show that compensation in the cell alone is not sufficient:
90\% transmission into the inflector acceptance needs a downstream compensation of
\numstCWtwoetaninety--0.9 along the solenoid and quadrupoles, whereas the electron retention
there limits residual-gas compensation at $\numpHtwo$~Torr to $\lesssim\numstCWthreeetasol$.
Bunched-beam simulations show that the electrons do not follow strong bunches, so only the
RF-averaged compensation applies, and a sine-bunched beam from the baseline buncher position
delivers only \numstBfiveGbasea{} of the DC accepted current. The design therefore hinges on
electron confinement downstream of the cell and on where and how the beam is bunched.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

% =====================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Compact cyclotrons for isotope production and accelerator-driven applications are
pushed toward average beam currents of several mA and beyond. In a compact machine the
beam is produced by an external ion source and injected axially through a spiral
inflector. At the typical injection energy of tens of keV the beam is strongly
space-charge dominated, and the transverse and longitudinal space-charge forces in the
injection line and on the first turns set practical intensity limits~\cite{Baartman1995}.

In low-energy beam transport (LEBT) lines, positive ion beams ionize the residual gas.
Secondary electrons are trapped in the beam potential, and secondary ions are
expelled, so the beam space charge is progressively compensated~\cite{Gabovich1977,Reiser2008}.
Compensation degrees above 90\% are routinely reported for DC beams in magnetic
LEBTs~\cite{Chauvin2012,BenIsmail2007}, while partial compensation and its dependence
on gas species and pressure have been measured and simulated in detail for both positive
and negative ion beams~\cite{ValerioLizarraga2015,Soloshenko2004}. In cyclotron injector
lines, measured compensation ranges from 0 to 60\%, depending on beam intensity,
radius and pressure~\cite{Winklehner2013}.

Compact axial injection lines differ from these LEBTs in two respects. First, they
are short: there is little drift length over which a compensating electron population
can build up. Second, the beam is bunched upstream of the injection optics, so
the beam potential that traps electrons is modulated at the RF frequency. Dedicated
electron columns, in which the beam ionizes a short, locally pressurized gas section
and the resulting electrons are shaped by external solenoid and electrode fields, have
been proposed and simulated for space-charge compensation in rings~\cite{Freemire2018,Park2020}.

This paper evaluates the same idea for compact-cyclotron injection. We consider a
compact beam-ionized $\Htwo$ or Kr gas cell placed upstream of the main solenoid,
\begin{multline*}
\text{buncher}\rightarrow\text{plasma neutralizer}\rightarrow\text{solenoid}\\
\rightarrow\text{Q1}\rightarrow\text{Q2}\rightarrow\text{spiral inflector},
\end{multline*}
and ask what neutralization it can provide, on what time scale, and under which
confinement conditions. Section~\ref{sec:concept} defines the design point.
Section~\ref{sec:model} develops closed-form estimates for perveance, ionization,
confinement and bunched-beam effects. Section~\ref{sec:methods} describes the
WarpX/PICMI simulation framework, the transport and bunching models and the
verification plan. Section~\ref{sec:results} presents the analytical results, the production
PIC results for a DC beam, the electron-confinement studies, transport to the inflector and
the bunched beam, and Sec.~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses design implications and limitations.

\section{Beamline and neutralizer concept}
\label{sec:concept}

Figure~\ref{fig:layout} shows the baseline layout. The neutralizer is a gas cell of
length $L=\numLcellcm$~cm filled with $\Htwo$ or Kr at a controlled pressure in the
$10^{-6}$--$10^{-5}$~Torr range, with optional local solenoid field and end electrodes
for electron confinement. It is placed after the buncher so that it acts on the beam
before the main solenoid focuses it. Table~\ref{tab:params} lists the design-point
parameters used throughout this paper.

\section{Analytical model}
\label{sec:model}

\subsection{Perveance and envelope growth}

For a round beam of particles with charge $q$, mass $m$ and velocity $v=\beta c$, the
generalized perveance is~\cite{Reiser2008}
\begin{equation}
K_0=\frac{qI}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 m v^3\gamma^3},
\label{eq:K0}
\end{equation}
which gives $K_0=\numKzero$ at the design point. The edge radius $a(z)$ of a uniform
round beam in a field-free drift obeys the envelope equation
\begin{equation}
a''=\frac{\Keff}{a}+\frac{\varepsilon^2}{a^3},
\qquad \Keff = K_0\,(1-\eta_{\mathrm{net}}),
\label{eq:envelope}
\end{equation}
where $\varepsilon$ is the edge emittance and
\begin{equation}
\eta_{\mathrm{net}}=\frac{n_e-n_i}{n_b}
\label{eq:eta}
\end{equation}
is the local net neutralization fraction evaluated in the beam core. For a parallel,
zero-emittance beam, Eq.~\eqref{eq:envelope} integrates exactly. The radius doubles after
\begin{equation}
z_2=\frac{a_0}{\sqrt{2\Keff}}\int_1^2\frac{dx}{\sqrt{\ln x}},
\label{eq:z2}
\end{equation}
which is $\numzdoublecm$~cm for $\Keff=K_0$, i.e.\ shorter than the neutralizer
itself. Figure~\ref{fig:envelope}(a) shows $a(z)$ over the cell length. An
uncompensated beam grows by a factor \numgrowthKzero{}; reducing $\Keff/K_0$ to 0.5 and
0.1 reduces the growth factor to \numgrowthKhalf{} and \numgrowthKtenth{},
respectively. These numbers are upper bounds on the growth, because the laminar
model ignores the emittance term and assumes the full perveance acts from $z=0$, but
they show that useful compensation must be established within a few centimetres of the
cell entrance.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{fig4_envelope_drift}
\caption{Laminar envelope $a(z)/a_0$ of a parallel, zero-emittance beam in a
\numLcellcm-cm drift [Eq.~\eqref{eq:envelope}, $\varepsilon=0$] for several
$\Keff/K_0$. (a)~DC slice at $I_{\mathrm{avg}}$. (b)~Peak slice at
$B_f I_{\mathrm{avg}}$; the dashed line is the static-background bound
$\Keff/K_{0}=1-\etaavg/B_f$ with $\etaavg=0.9$. The slice model neglects the finite
bunch length (\numbunchmm~mm) and overestimates the peak-slice growth.}
\label{fig:envelope}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{Ionization source and cross sections}

Secondary electrons are produced by proton-impact ionization,
$p^+ + X\rightarrow p^+ + X^+ + e^-$, with $X=\Htwo$ or Kr. We use total
ionization cross sections from the Rudd semi-empirical model~\cite{Rudd1985,Rudd1992},
tabulated on a uniform center-of-mass energy grid for use in WarpX MCC
[Fig.~\ref{fig:xs}(a)]. The cross section depends on the projectile velocity. The
tables are therefore evaluated at the 30-keV laboratory energy and stored at the
corresponding center-of-mass energies, $E_{\mathrm{cm}}=E_{\mathrm{lab}}\,m_X/(m_p+m_X)$
(20.0~keV for $\Htwo$ and 29.6~keV for Kr). At 30~keV,
$\sigma_{\Htwo}=\numsigmaHtwo$~m$^2$ and $\sigma_{\mathrm{Kr}}=\numsigmaKr$~m$^2$, a
ratio of \numsigmaratio. At this energy the model lies in the low-energy region where
Rudd \emph{et al.}\ report discrepancies between data sets for some targets~\cite{Rudd1983}.
\pending{Quantitative comparison of the tabulated values with the measurements of
Ref.~\cite{Rudd1983}, and the resulting uncertainty band.}

The ionization rate per proton is $n_g\sigma v$, so the characteristic build-up time
of the electron population is
\begin{equation}
\tau_{\mathrm{ion}}=\frac{1}{n_g\,\sigma\,v}.
\label{eq:tau}
\end{equation}
With $n_g=p/k_BT_g$ this gives $\tau_{\mathrm{ion}}=\numtauHtwous~\mu$s for $\Htwo$ at
$\numpHtwo$~Torr ($n_g=\numnHtwo$~m$^{-3}$) and $\numtauKrus~\mu$s for Kr at
$\numpKr$~Torr [Fig.~\ref{fig:xs}(b)]. Because the cross-section ratio
(\numsigmaratio) is smaller than the pressure ratio (10), Kr at $\numpKr$~Torr builds
up \emph{more slowly} than $\Htwo$ at $\numpHtwo$~Torr. Equal build-up times require
$p_{\mathrm{Kr}}=p_{\Htwo}\sigma_{\Htwo}/\sigma_{\mathrm{Kr}}=\numpKrequal$~Torr.
The single-pass ionization probability across the cell, $n_g\sigma L$, is
$\numPionHtwo$ for $\Htwo$ and $\numPionKr$ for Kr.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{fig2_cross_sections_tau}
\caption{(a)~Rudd-model proton-impact ionization cross sections of $\Htwo$ and Kr
versus proton laboratory energy; dots mark 30~keV. (b)~Ionization build-up time
[Eq.~\eqref{eq:tau}] versus pressure at 300~K. Circle: $\Htwo$ at $\numpHtwo$~Torr;
square: Kr at $\numpKr$~Torr; cross: Kr pressure giving the same $\tau_{\mathrm{ion}}$
as the $\Htwo$ design point.}
\label{fig:xs}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{Neutralization balance and electron confinement}

The commonly used build-up law $\eta(t)=\eta_{\mathrm{ss}}[1-\exp(-t/\tau_{\mathrm{ion}})]$
contains the steady-state value $\eta_{\mathrm{ss}}$ as a free parameter. In a simple
particle balance per unit length,
\begin{equation}
\frac{dN_e}{dt}=\frac{N_p}{\tau_{\mathrm{ion}}}-\frac{N_e}{\tau_c},
\qquad
\eta_{\mathrm{ss}}\simeq\min\!\left(1,\frac{\tau_c}{\tau_{\mathrm{ion}}}\right),
\label{eq:balance}
\end{equation}
$\eta_{\mathrm{ss}}$ is set by the electron confinement time $\tau_c$ in the beam
core. Real equilibria are self-limiting: as $\eta\to1$ the trapping well vanishes, so
$\eta_{\mathrm{ss}}<1$ even for long $\tau_c$~\cite{Gabovich1977}.

Transversely, the uncompensated beam potential confines electrons with a well depth
\begin{equation}
\Delta\Phi=\frac{\lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[1+2\ln\frac{b}{a}\right]
\label{eq:well}
\end{equation}
equal to \numwellavg~V at the average line density, much larger than the
\numEeev-eV secondary-electron energy we assume. Longitudinally, the beam potential
inside a short cell is uniform, so electrons are free to stream out of the gas region.
A \numEeev-eV electron leaves the \numLcellcm-cm cell in about \numtescapens~ns. With
$\tau_c$ equal to this time, Eq.~\eqref{eq:balance} gives a cell-local neutralization of only
$\eta\sim\numetafreeHtwo$ ($\Htwo$) and $\numetafreeKr$ (Kr). The electrons are not lost;
they spread over the whole length between the electron-clearing elements of the line.
The local compensation in a compact cell therefore depends on longitudinal confinement,
for example by electrostatic end plugs, or on the cell being part of a longer
compensated section. This is the central design requirement identified here.

Slow ions are expelled radially by the beam field. An ion born at rest at $r_0=a/2$ in
a uniform beam follows $r(t)=r_0\cosh(t/t_i)$, with
$t_i=\sqrt{2\pi\varepsilon_0a^2M/(e\lambda)}$, and reaches the beam edge after
\numtexpelHtwons~ns ($\Htwo^+$) or \numtexpelKrns~ns (Kr$^+$). The resulting ion
contribution to Eq.~\eqref{eq:eta}, $N_i/N_p\approx t_{\mathrm{exp}}/\tau_{\mathrm{ion}}$,
is $\numionfracHtwo$ for $\Htwo$ and $\numionfracKr$ for Kr. It is negligible while the
beam is far from compensation and grows as the well collapses.

\subsection{RF-bunched beam}

The buncher precedes the neutralizer, so the cell sees bunches with RF period
$T_{\mathrm{RF}}=\numTRFns$~ns. A \numdphideg$^\circ$ phase width corresponds to a
bunch duration of \numbunchns~ns, a bunch length of \numbunchmm~mm, and a gap of
\numgapns~ns. A uniformly filled \numdphideg$^\circ$ bunch would have $B_f=\numBfuniform$.
Here $B_f$ is treated as a free parameter, with $B_f=\numBf$ as the reference value.

If the electron background is static at the average-compensating density $\etaavg n_b$,
the peak-bunch net charge gives
\begin{equation}
\frac{K_{\mathrm{eff,peak}}}{K_{0,\mathrm{peak}}}\simeq1-\frac{\etaavg}{B_f},
\label{eq:peak}
\end{equation}
shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:peak}. For $\etaavg=0.9$ and $B_f=\numBf$ the peak-bunch
perveance is reduced only to \numKeffpeakstatic{} of its uncompensated value
$K_{0,\mathrm{peak}}=\numKzeropeak$. Figure~\ref{fig:envelope}(b) shows that this
reduction barely changes the peak-slice envelope.

\begin{figure}[tb]
\includegraphics[width=0.8\columnwidth]{fig5_peak_perveance}
\caption{Peak-bunch perveance ratio for a static electron background,
Eq.~\eqref{eq:peak}. Dotted lines: $B_f=\numBf$ (reference) and
$B_f=\numBfuniform$ (uniform \numdphideg$^\circ$ bunch).}
\label{fig:peak}
\end{figure}

Equation~\eqref{eq:peak} rests on a static background, which is not guaranteed in either
direction. The electron plasma frequency at the peak bunch density is
$\omega_{pe}=\numomegapepeak$~rad/s, so $\omega_{pe}\Delta t_b\approx\numomegapebunch$.
Electrons can therefore respond within one bunch, and confined electrons could
partially follow the bunch structure and exceed the bound in Eq.~\eqref{eq:peak}. Conversely, during
the \numgapns-ns gap the beam potential is absent while a \numEeev-eV electron crosses
the beam radius in \numtcrossns~ns. Without external confinement, the electron column
accumulated during a bunch is therefore lost before the next bunch arrives, and even
$\etaavg$ cannot be sustained. Holding the electrons transversely during the gap
requires a Larmor radius well below $a$. Taking $r_L=a/10$ for \numEeev-eV electrons gives
$B_z\approx\numBconfine$~mT, which motivates the optional local solenoid field of the
cell. The bunched-beam simulations of Sec.~\ref{sec:bunched} test both effects.

\subsection{Time-scale hierarchy}

Figure~\ref{fig:timescales} collects the relevant time scales. They span seven orders
of magnitude, from the plasma period to the ionization time. Two consequences
follow. First, the bunch-gap and electron-crossing times make confinement, not
ionization, the limiting process. Second, the ionization time exceeds the affordable
3D PIC run duration by more than two orders of magnitude (Sec.~\ref{sec:methods}),
so the steady state cannot be reached by direct simulation of the build-up.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\includegraphics[width=0.72\textwidth]{fig3_timescales}
\caption{Characteristic time scales at the design point: electron plasma period at
peak beam density, electron crossing and escape times (\numEeev-eV secondaries),
bunch structure, ion expulsion, proton transit, PIC run durations, and ionization
build-up times.}
\label{fig:timescales}
\end{figure*}

\section{Simulation methods}
\label{sec:methods}

\subsection{Code and model hierarchy}

Simulations use WarpX~\cite{Vay2021}, built on AMReX~\cite{Zhang2019}, driven through
its PICMI Python interface. Each case is launched as a separate process from a YAML case
file, and a metadata record (repository and WarpX commits, environment, command line,
gas, pressure, geometry, fields, beam and numerical parameters) is written with every
run. Four model levels are distinguished:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Vacuum reference}: no gas and no compensating species.
\item \emph{Seeded compensation}: an electron/ion population is initialized in the
cell at a density given by the build-up law with a prescribed $\eta_{\mathrm{ss}}$.
This is an analytic source estimate, not a self-consistent ionization model.
\item \emph{Python-callback source}: electron-ion pairs are created each step at the
analytic rate $n_g\sigma v$ by the beam macroparticles, with unbiased weight sampling.
This is a data-driven source model.
\item \emph{Custom proton-impact MCC}: a C++ extension of the WarpX background-MCC
module adds an ion-impact ionization process, whose filter and transform functors
create an $e^-$/ion pair from the projectile proton without slowing it.
\end{enumerate}
WarpX's built-in MCC impact ionization is designed for electron-impact
processes~\cite{Vahedi1995}. Level~4 therefore depends on the custom extension, which is
maintained as a patch against WarpX and is not yet validated (Sec.~\ref{sec:verification}).
The present production driver supports levels 1--3, optionally with built-in
electron-impact ionization of the seeded electrons and proton charge exchange on $\Htwo$.

In the seeded model the plasma occupies $r\le3$~mm over the cell length, with equal
electron and ion densities $n_e=n_i=f\,n_b$ at $t=0$ ($n_b$: nominal uniform beam density).
The seed fraction is taken from the build-up law with $\eta_{\mathrm{ss}}=0.9$ evaluated
200~$\mu$s after beam turn-on, $f=0.9[1-\exp(-200~\mu\mathrm{s}/\tau_{\mathrm{ion}})]$, so
it rises with pressure and saturates at 0.9 (Table~\ref{tab:pic}). The beam is then injected
into this plasma. The run therefore follows the redistribution of a prescribed plasma by the
beam field, not its creation.

At the physical rate, level~3 creates a fraction $1-\exp(-t/\tau_{\mathrm{ion}})\approx
\numpicovertau$ of the steady-state population within a PIC run. It is therefore not part of
the production matrix. A single run with the ionization rate multiplied by 1000
($\tau_{\mathrm{eff}}=\numpicacctaueffns$~ns, labeled \emph{rescaled} in all outputs)
tests the dynamic build-up. Level~4 production cases use the built-in electron-impact MCC
on the seeded plasma (``e-MCC''); proton-impact MCC is not used.

\subsection{Numerical parameters}

The baseline 3D Cartesian domain spans $|x|,|y|\le10$~mm and $-2\le z\le24$~cm on a
$64\times64\times512$ grid, which resolves the beam radius with about six cells. The cell
($0\le z\le20$~cm) has a uniform 0.15~T hard-edge solenoid field. The fields are computed
by an electrostatic FFT Poisson solver with open boundaries, which is adequate for the
non-relativistic ($\beta=\numbeta$) beam and removes the light-wave Courant limit. The
time step is then set by electron gyration, $\omega_{ce}\Delta t=0.25$, so
$\Delta t=\numpicdtps$~ps. A run of \numpicsteps{} steps covers \numpicns~ns, i.e.\ two
transits of the domain and \numpicovertransit{} transits of the cell, but only $\numpicovertau$
of $\tau_{\mathrm{ion}}$ for $\Htwo$. The DC beam (\numIavgma~mA, \numEkev~keV, $a=\numabeammm$~mm)
is injected at $z=-2$~cm with four macroparticles per cell (weight $\approx1.2\times10^3$);
the plasma uses 16 macroparticles per cell. On a $32\times32\times256$ grid over a matched
28~ns window, the electrostatic solver reproduces electromagnetic global particle counts
within 1\% and local core values within about 10\% at 1/14 of the step count.
\pending{Convergence of the electron confinement time in grid size, macroparticles per cell
and $\Delta t$ (task 123, running).}

\subsection{Confinement, transport and bunching models}
\label{sec:studymodels}

\emph{Confinement runs} use the seeded model on a $32\times32\times256$ grid at the
production time step for \numstCOtend~ns, with the cell solenoid field $B_z$, the seed
electron temperature $T_e$ and electrostatic end plugs (ring electrodes of width $w$ at
voltage $-V$) as parameters. The confinement time $\tau_c$ is fitted to the decay of the
electron number in the cell over the second half of the run. The best configuration is
repeated on the production grid with a longer domain ($-7\le z\le27$~cm) for
\numstCWtendns~ns. A \emph{guiding-centre test-electron model} follows electrons in the
static fields of the same trap (plugs, solenoid and the compensated beam well) with elastic
e-$\Htwo$ collisions and beam heating for \numstCtwotend~$\mu$s, which PIC cannot reach.

\emph{Transport to the inflector} uses the KV envelope equations through the cell, the
main solenoid and the Q1/Q2 doublet, with the cell compensation from the PIC runs and a
uniform downstream compensation $\eta_{\mathrm{down}}$ as a parameter; the solenoid and
quadrupole strengths are rematched for each case. Transmission is a geometric estimate of the
beam fraction inside the 10~mm pipe and inside the inflector acceptance (5~mm radius,
50~mrad). Two-dimensional particle tracking
with space charge checks the envelope result for KV and Gaussian beams and transports the
macroparticles taken from the PIC cell exit.

\emph{Electron retention downstream} is computed with a WarpX section model of the line
(solenoid with fringe field, hard-edge quadrupoles) filled with a seeded residual-gas plasma
at $\numpHtwo$~Torr. An axisymmetric Poisson model sizes an electron suppressor ring before
the inflector; the inflector field is represented by an illustrative leakage potential.

\emph{Bunched beams} are modeled in PIC with a von Mises current profile at $B_f=1.3$ (the
bunching at the cell for the baseline buncher) and $B_f=5$ (a bunch-focus study), in the cell
and in the line section. Transport of the bunch uses nine 4$^\circ$ slices of the
36$^\circ$ inflector acceptance window, each with its local current from ballistic bunching,
through common matched optics. Compensation enters either RF-averaged,
$\Keff=K_0(B_s-\etaavg)$ for a slice with local current factor $B_s$, or per slice,
$\Keff=K_0B_s(1-\eta)$, which is an upper bound. The figure of merit is the accepted-current
gain over a DC beam, $G=\sum_s f_sT_s/(0.1\,T_{\mathrm{DC}})$, with $f_s$ the current
fraction and $T_s$ the transmission of slice $s$. Buncher positions other than the cell
entrance are an \emph{alternative-placement study}.

\subsection{Diagnostics}

Global particle counts $N_p$, $N_e$, $N_i$ are recorded every few steps. A global
ratio $N_e/N_p$ includes electrons outside the beam and outside the cell. We
therefore base all compensation claims on the local diagnostic
\begin{equation}
\eta_{\mathrm{local,net}}=\frac{\langle n_e\rangle-\langle n_i\rangle}{\langle n_b\rangle},
\end{equation}
where the averages are taken over $r\le a$ inside the cell, restricted to cells that
contain beam protons so that cells not yet reached by the beam front do not dilute
$\langle n_b\rangle$. They are evaluated from full 3D snapshots every 2300 steps
(21.8~ns). For bunched beams we report the RF-period average, the peak-bunch value and the
local value separately.

\subsection{Verification plan}
\label{sec:verification}

The custom MCC extension will be checked against analytic targets: no ionization
without gas or with $\sigma=0$; a fixed-cross-section rate $dN_e/dt=N_pn_g\sigma v$;
the Kr/$\Htwo$ yield ratio equal to $\sigma_{\mathrm{Kr}}/\sigma_{\Htwo}$ at equal
density; convergence of the per-step probability $P=1-\exp(-n_g\sigma v\Delta t)$ for
$\Delta t$, $\Delta t/2$, $\Delta t/4$; conservation of physical particle number under
macroparticle weighting; and secondary-electron energy bookkeeping.
\pending{Execution of these tests with the patched WarpX build; the WarpX build used
must be shown to match the archived patch.}

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Analytical design results}

The analytical results of Sec.~\ref{sec:model} are summarized below:
\begin{itemize}
\item An uncompensated \numIavgma-mA beam doubles its radius in \numzdoublecm~cm and
grows by \numgrowthKzero$\times$ over the cell. Compensation must therefore be
established near the cell entrance.
\item Ionization build-up takes \numtauHtwous~$\mu$s ($\Htwo$, $\numpHtwo$~Torr) and
\numtauKrus~$\mu$s (Kr, $\numpKr$~Torr). Kr matches $\Htwo$ at $\numpKrequal$~Torr.
\item Without longitudinal confinement, cell-local neutralization is limited to
$\sim10^{-3}$ by electron escape.
\item For a bunched beam, transverse electron confinement during the \numgapns-ns gap
requires $B_z\sim\numBconfine$~mT or equivalent.
\item With an ideal static background, peak-bunch perveance is reduced only to
\numKeffpeakstatic{} of its uncompensated value ($\etaavg=0.9$, $B_f=\numBf$).
\end{itemize}

\subsection{PIC results for a DC beam}
\label{sec:picresults}

The production matrix contains \numpicncases{} cases: a vacuum reference; seeded $\Htwo$ and
Kr columns at six pressures from $10^{-6}$ to $3\times10^{-4}$~Torr; and the two design
pressures repeated with electron-impact MCC (Table~\ref{tab:pic}). All cases use the
numerics of Sec.~\ref{sec:methods} and run \numpicsteps{} steps (\numpicns~ns). The beam front
reaches the end of the cell before half of the run; the values in Table~\ref{tab:pic} are
taken at \numpicns~ns, when the beam fills every core cell.

Figure~\ref{fig:pictime}(a) shows the core neutralization during the run. At
$\numpHtwo$~Torr $\Htwo$ (seed fraction \numpicHtwoseed), $\eta_{\mathrm{net}}$ rises to about 1
once the beam fills the cell and settles at \numpicHtwoeta{} ($\Keff/K_0=\numpicHtwokeff$). For Kr at
$\numpKr$~Torr (seed fraction \numpicKrseed) it reaches only \numpicKreta. The vacuum
reference stays at zero. Adding electron-impact MCC changes $\eta_{\mathrm{net}}$ by about
0.01 or less (\numpicHtwomcceta{} and \numpicKrmcceta). This is expected: at these pressures
the probability that a seed electron ionizes the gas within the run is below $10^{-4}$.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{fig6_pic_eta_vs_time}
\caption{Beam-core neutralization versus time from the 3D snapshots. (a)~Seeded plasma at
the design pressures, with and without electron-impact MCC, and the vacuum reference.
Early points have partially filled cores. (b)~Dynamic build-up with the Python-callback
source at $\numpHtwo$~Torr $\Htwo$. This run is \emph{rescaled}: the ionization rate is multiplied by
1000 ($\tau_{\mathrm{eff}}=\numpicacctaueffns$~ns). The dashed curve is the fraction of the
steady-state source integrated so far.}
\label{fig:pictime}
\end{figure*}

The difference between the gases is in the ions. Figure~\ref{fig:picprofiles} shows the
radial profiles at \numpicns~ns. In $\Htwo$, only \numpicHtwoniseed{} of the seeded ion
density remains in the core; the ions have been pushed to the edge of the beam and beyond,
and the electrons ($n_e/n_b=\numpicHtwone$) are almost neutralized by the beam alone. In Kr,
\numpicKrniseed{} of the seeded ions remain, and the electron density rises to
$\numpicKrne\,n_b$ to compensate both beam and ions, leaving $\eta_{\mathrm{net}}=\numpicKreta$.
This agrees with the expulsion times of Sec.~\ref{sec:model}: \numtexpelHtwons~ns for
$\Htwo^+$ but \numtexpelKrns~ns for Kr$^+$, longer than the run. The weaker compensation also
lets the Kr beam expand: the core beam density is \numpicKrnbcore{} of the nominal $n_b$,
compared with \numpicHtwonbcore{} for $\Htwo$. Electrons exceed the beam density in every
seeded case at or above the design pressures, so $\Keff/K_0$ based on electrons alone would
be negative; the net value never is.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{fig8_pic_radial_profiles}
\caption{Radial density profiles averaged over the cell at \numpicns~ns for the seeded

Figure~\ref{fig:picpressure} shows the pressure scans. For $\Htwo$, $\eta_{\mathrm{net}}$
follows the seed fraction from \numpicHtwoetalowp{} at $10^{-6}$~Torr ($f=\numpicHtwoseedlowp$)
and \numpicHtwoetamidp{} at $3\times10^{-6}$~Torr ($f=\numpicHtwoseedmidp$) to
\numpicHtwoplateaumin{} from $10^{-5}$~Torr upward, where $f$ saturates. It exceeds $f$
because electrons from the 3-mm seeded column collect in the 2-mm beam while ions leave. For
Kr, $\eta_{\mathrm{net}}$ stays between \numpicKretamin{} and \numpicKretamax{}, while
$n_i/n_b$ stays between \numpicKrnimin{} and \numpicKrnimax{}, even though $f$ rises to
\numpicKrseedmax. On this time scale, raising the Kr pressure adds ions that cannot leave,
and the net compensation does not improve.

The rescaled callback run [Fig.~\ref{fig:pictime}(b)] tests the build-up instead of a
prescribed plasma. Pairs are created at the sampled rate to within 0.1\% of the expected
weight. The core electron density follows and exceeds the source integral, reaching
$\numpicaccne\,n_b$ when $1-\exp(-t/\tau_{\mathrm{eff}})=\numpicaccsource$. The newly created
$\Htwo^+$ ions are still accumulating, so $\eta_{\mathrm{net}}$ reaches \numpicacceta{} and is still
rising. Because the rate is artificial, this run shows the mechanism, not the time scale.

The global ratio $(N_e-N_i)/N_p$ over the whole domain is only \numpicHtwoglobal{} for the
$\Htwo$ design case, against \numpicHtwoeta{} in the core. This confirms that global particle
counts cannot be used to claim local compensation.

\subsection{Electron confinement in the cell}
\label{sec:confinement}

Figure~\ref{fig:confinement} collects the fitted confinement times. Without a magnetic field
the electrons leave the cell with $\tau_c=\numstCOtauBzero~\mu$s; the 0.15~T cell solenoid
raises this to \numstCOtauBhigh~$\mu$s ($T_e=1$~eV). Narrow (5~mm) end plugs at 300~V do the
opposite: they shorten $\tau_c$ by a factor \numstCOplugratiomin--\numstCOplugratiomax{} in
every case of the scan, and the strong lens field of the plug triples the exit divergence of
the beam (\numstCthreedivnoplug{} to \numstCthreedivplug~mrad) and raises its rms emittance
\numstCthreeremit-fold. Wider plugs behave differently. At 300~V, plugs of 10 and 20~mm width
give $\tau_c=\numstCFtauwten$ and \numstCFtauwtwenty~$\mu$s, against \numstCFtaunoplug~$\mu$s
without plugs and \numstCFtauwfive~$\mu$s with 5~mm plugs in the same longer domain, while the
divergence at the cell end grows by only \numstCFdivincrmin--\numstCFdivincrmax\%.

The selected configuration (0.15~T, 1~eV, 300~V, 10~mm plugs) on the production grid keeps
the core compensation at $\eta_{\mathrm{net}}=\numstCWeta$ (range
\numstCWetamin--\numstCWetamax) from \numstCWfromns{} to \numstCWtendns~ns, with
$\tau_c=\numstCWtauc~\mu$s. The beam leaves the domain with
$r_{\mathrm{rms}}=\numstCWrexit$~mm and \numstCWdivexit~mrad; most of this divergence is
produced in the uncompensated drift before the cell.

The PIC confinement times are short compared with the guiding-centre test-electron result.
In the static trap with plugs of 100~V or more, at least \numstCtwosurvmin{} of the test
electrons survive \numstCtwotend~$\mu$s, for well depths down to \numstCtwowellmin~V, while
they heat to \numstCtwoenergylow~eV (1~eV birth) or \numstCtwoenergyhigh~eV (10~eV birth).
Without plugs they leave in \numstCtwoopentaumin--\numstCtwoopentaumax~$\mu$s, close to the
PIC values. The electron loss in the plugged PIC runs is therefore caused by collective or
numerical effects absent from the test-particle model, and the PIC $\tau_c$ is a lower bound
until its convergence is shown.
\pending{Convergence of $\tau_c$ with grid, macroparticles per cell and time step (task 123).}

\begin{figure}[tb]
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig9_confinement_times}
\caption{Fitted electron confinement times from the seeded PIC runs: the cell with and without
end plugs (DC beam), the cell trap and the main solenoid with a bunched beam, and the
solenoid and quadrupoles of the line section at $\numpHtwo$~Torr. Dashed: the $\tau_c$
needed for $\eta_{\mathrm{ss}}=0.7$ at $\numpHtwo$~Torr $\Htwo$ [Eq.~\eqref{eq:balance}].}
\label{fig:confinement}
\end{figure}

\paragraph*{Steady state.} The seeded runs show that a confined plasma compensates the beam;
they do not show that the gas can maintain it. In the balance of Eq.~\eqref{eq:balance}
with $\tau_{\mathrm{ion}}=\numstSStauion~\mu$s, the two confinement results bracket the
steady state. With the PIC value $\tau_c=\numstCWtauc~\mu$s, $\eta_{\mathrm{ss}}\approx
\numstCWetass$, reached after about \numstSSbuildpic~$\mu$s. With the test-electron result
($\tau_c\gg\tau_{\mathrm{ion}}$), $\eta_{\mathrm{ss}}$ is limited only by the collapse of the
well, and $\eta=0.9$ is reached after about \numstSSbuildninety~$\mu$s. A self-consistent
build-up simulation would decide between the two; it requires the validated proton-impact
source of Sec.~\ref{sec:verification} and is left for future work.

\subsection{Transport to the inflector}
\label{sec:transport}

Figure~\ref{fig:transmission} shows the transmission into the inflector acceptance as a
function of the downstream compensation, with the cell compensation fixed at the CW1 value.
For a normalized edge emittance of 0.25~$\pi$~mm~mrad, an uncompensated line transmits
\numstCWtwoTzero; $T\ge0.5$ needs $\eta_{\mathrm{down}}\ge\numstCWtwoetahalf$ and $T\ge0.9$
needs $\eta_{\mathrm{down}}\ge\numstCWtwoetaninety$. At 0.5~$\pi$~mm~mrad transmission
saturates at \numstCWtwoTmidemit{}, and at 1.0~$\pi$~mm~mrad the beam is emittance-dominated
($T\le\numstCWtwoThighemit$). Particle tracking of a KV beam agrees with the envelope to within
\numstCWfiveKVdev{} for $\eta_{\mathrm{down}}\ge0.5$. A Gaussian beam of the same rms
emittance loses its tails: $T=\numstCWfiveGseven$ and \numstCWfiveGnine{} at
$\eta_{\mathrm{down}}=0.7$ and 0.9, so about 0.9 is needed in practice. The macroparticle beam
from the CW1 cell exit reaches only $T=\numstCWfivepicmin$--\numstCWfivepicmax{} because it
leaves the cell too wide; a beam injected closer to the cell reaches \numstCWfiveshortnine{} at
$\eta_{\mathrm{down}}=0.9$. The CW1 runs used a hard-edge cell solenoid, which does not focus,
so this result is pessimistic.

\begin{figure}[tb]
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig10_transmission_downstream}
\caption{Transmission into the inflector acceptance versus uniform downstream compensation,
cell compensation from CW1. Lines: KV envelope for three normalized edge emittances. Open
symbols: Gaussian beams tracked with space charge. Diamonds: macroparticles from the CW1 PIC
cell exit, tracked with rematched optics.}
\label{fig:transmission}
\end{figure}

Can residual gas provide this downstream compensation? The section model gives
$\tau_c=\numstCWthreesolmin$--\numstCWthreesolmax~$\mu$s in the main solenoid (fringe field
included; \numstCWthreenofields~$\mu$s without fields) and
\numstCWthreequadmin--\numstCWthreequadmax~$\mu$s in the quadrupoles, which do not trap
electrons (Fig.~\ref{fig:confinement}). At $\numpHtwo$~Torr this gives
$\eta_{\mathrm{ss}}\approx\numstCWthreeetasolmin$--\numstCWthreeetasol{} in the solenoid and
$<0.01$ in the quadrupoles, far below the 0.7--0.9 required. Reaching 0.7 with these
confinement times would need about $\numstCWthreepsol$~Torr in the solenoid and
$\numstCWthreepquad$~Torr in the quadrupoles, where gas scattering and charge exchange must be
assessed. Electrons that are held in the line must also be kept out of the inflector field: a
suppressor ring before the inflector needs $-\numstCWfourVsmalla$, $-\numstCWfourVsmallb$ and
$-\numstCWfourVsmallc$~V (5~mm aperture) or $-\numstCWfourVlargea$ to $-\numstCWfourVlargec$~V
(7.5~mm) for a 20~V barrier at $\eta_{\mathrm{down}}=0.5$, 0.7 and 0.9, and its lens effect on
the beam is negligible (focal length $\ge\numstCWfourfocalmin$~km).

\subsection{Bunched beam}
\label{sec:bunched}

In the cell, the bunching from the baseline buncher position is weak ($B_{\mathrm{cell}}=
\numstBtwoBcell$ for $B_f=1.3$). With the trap, the RF-averaged compensation stays at
\numstBtwoetabase{} (DC: \numstBtwoetadc), but $\tau_c$ falls from \numstBtwotaudc{} to
\numstBtwotaubase~$\mu$s. Without plugs it is \numstBtwoetaopen{} with
$\tau_c=\numstBtwotauopen~\mu$s. The peak-bunch value, \numstBtwopeakbase, cannot be
separated from the average at this modulation (snapshot spread \numstBtwopeakstd). A strongly
bunched beam ($B_f=5$, a bunch-focus study) empties the trap within $\tau_c=
\numstBtwotaufocus~\mu$s and leaves an ion excess ($\etaavg=\numstBtwoetafocus$).

Downstream, where the bunching grows toward the inflector, the section model with $B_f=3$ and
5.7 shows that the electrons do not follow the bunches. The peak-bunch compensation equals the
static-cloud value $\etaavg/B_{\mathrm{cell}}$ of Eq.~\eqref{eq:peak}:
\numstBfourpeaka{} against \numstBfourstatica{} at $B_{\mathrm{cell}}=\numstBfourBcella$ and
\numstBfourpeakb{} against \numstBfourstaticb{} at $B_{\mathrm{cell}}=\numstBfourBcellb$, and
$\tau_c$ in the solenoid drops to \numstBfourtaua{} and \numstBfourtaub~$\mu$s. The
RF-averaged compensation model is therefore the relevant one, not the per-slice bound.

Figure~\ref{fig:gain} shows what this means for the accepted current. With the sine buncher at
the cell entrance ($B_f=\numstBfiveBf$ in the 36$^\circ$ window at the inflector) the slices
pass through a crossover with a local current factor of up to \numstBfiveslicebase{} before the
inflector, and the accepted current is only $G=\numstBfiveGbasea$, \numstBfiveGbaseb{} and
\numstBfiveGbasec{} of a DC beam for $\eta_{\mathrm{down}}=0$, 0.5 and 0.9. Even the per-slice
bound gives only \numstBfiveboundbase. Moving the buncher downstream is an
alternative-placement study: between Q1 and Q2 ($\numstBfiveVq$~kV) $G=\numstBfiveGqa$ to
\numstBfiveGqc, and between Q2 and the inflector ($\numstBfiveVlate$~kV, outside the range of
the ballistic model) $G=\numstBfiveGlateb$--\numstBfiveGlatea. An ideal sawtooth waveform
($B_f=\numstBsixBf$) avoids the crossover. At the cell entrance it gives $G=\numstBsixGbasea$
without downstream compensation, and between Q1 and Q2 ($\numstBsixVq$~kV) \numstBsixGqc--%
\numstBsixGqa. For upstream buncher positions $G$ decreases as $\eta_{\mathrm{down}}$ rises: RF-averaged
compensation removes at most $\etaavg$ from a slice perveance of $B_sK_0$, so the accepted bunch
current barely changes while the DC reference transmission rises from \numstCWtwoTzero{}
toward 1.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{fig11_bunched_gain}
\caption{Accepted-current gain over a DC beam for nine 4$^\circ$ slices of the 36$^\circ$
inflector window, normalized edge emittance 0.25~$\pi$~mm~mrad, for the buncher at the cell
entrance (baseline) and at two downstream positions (alternative-placement study).
(a)~Sine buncher. (b)~Ideal sawtooth. Symbols: RF-averaged compensation for three downstream
compensation levels; bars: per-slice upper bound at $\eta_{\mathrm{down}}=0.9$. Dotted: DC beam.}
\label{fig:gain}
\end{figure*}

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Gas choice.}
Kr offers a larger cross section per atom, but at the pressures usually quoted it does
not build up faster than $\Htwo$. Kr is also heavier, so Kr$^+$ ions stay in the beam
about six times longer, which raises the ion contribution to $\eta_{\mathrm{net}}$
near full compensation. The PIC runs show this directly: with a seeded plasma, Kr reaches
only $\eta_{\mathrm{net}}\approx\numpicKretamin$--\numpicKretamax{} within \numpicns~ns at
every pressure, whereas $\Htwo$ reaches \numpicHtwoeta. This comparison favors the gas whose
ions leave the beam quickly. It is a statement about a seeded plasma that starts with
$n_i=n_e$, however. In a column that builds up by ionization, ions are created gradually
and are expelled while the electrons accumulate, so the Kr penalty may be smaller. Testing
this requires the build-up simulations discussed under Limitations. Its gas load on the downstream cyclotron vacuum must also be
assessed. $\Htwo$ is chemically compatible with hydrogen ion sources. The choice
should be made at equal $\tau_{\mathrm{ion}}$ and should include charge-exchange beam
loss, for which measured capture cross sections are available~\cite{Rudd1983} but are
not yet included in our source model.
\pending{Charge-exchange loss and small-angle scattering estimates for both gases.
The Highland formula is not appropriate at keV energies; screened-Coulomb elastic
cross sections are required.}

\paragraph{Placement.}
Placing the cell before the solenoid lets it act on the beam before magnetic focusing.
The solenoid fringe field can contribute to transverse electron confinement, whereas
electrostatic elements and the buncher gap clear electrons and bound the compensated
section. Moving the neutralizer is outside the baseline design and is not considered here.
Moving the \emph{buncher} downstream is studied in Sec.~\ref{sec:bunched} as an explicitly
labeled alternative-placement study, because it is the only change that gives the bunched beam
a gain over a DC beam.

\paragraph{Downstream compensation.}
The cell is not the bottleneck. The PIC results show that a trapped column in the cell keeps
$\eta_{\mathrm{net}}\approx\numstCWeta$, but transport to the inflector needs
$\eta_{\mathrm{down}}\approx\numstCWtwoetaninety$--0.9 along the solenoid and the
quadrupoles as well, and residual gas at $\numpHtwo$~Torr provides
$\lesssim\numstCWthreeetasol$ there. Options are a higher local pressure in the solenoid
(about $\numstCWthreepsol$~Torr), electron traps (end electrodes) along the solenoid, or a
shorter uncompensated path between the cell and the inflector. Each must be checked against
scattering, charge exchange and the gas load on the cyclotron.

\paragraph{Overcompensation.}
Values of $\Keff/K_0<0$ correspond to net negative charge in the core and focus the
beam. They can arise transiently in seeded models with $\eta>1$ or in strongly confined
columns. Such values are always labeled explicitly. In the production runs the electron
density alone exceeds the beam density in most seeded cases, but the net core value stays
below 1 at \numpicns~ns; $\eta_{\mathrm{net}}$ briefly reaches unity in the
$\Htwo$ design case [Fig.~\ref{fig:pictime}(a)].

\paragraph{Limitations.}
The analytical results are closed-form estimates for a uniform round beam. The envelope
model is laminar and slice-based; the transport results use KV envelopes, geometric
transmission and a uniform downstream compensation, and the bunching model is ballistic
without longitudinal space charge, which would blunt the crossover. The confinement estimate uses a single
secondary-electron energy of \numEeev~eV. The bunched-beam bound assumes a static
background. Cross sections come from a semi-empirical model at the edge of its validated
range. The PIC results cover a DC beam for \numpicns~ns, i.e.\ $\numpicovertau\,\tau_{\mathrm{ion}}$.
They start from a prescribed plasma whose density follows the analytic build-up law, which
is an analytic source estimate and not self-consistent proton-impact ionization. The cell
has a uniform 0.15~T solenoid, which confines electrons transversely, and no end
electrodes. Electrons can leave the cell axially, but the free-escape time
(\numtescapens~ns) is about half the run, so axial losses are only partly developed. The
confinement studies run for \numstCOtend--\numstCWtendns~ns, so $\tau_c$ of several
$\mu$s is extrapolated from a partial decay, and the PIC values disagree with the
test-electron model; their convergence is being tested. The cell solenoid of the confinement
runs is hard-edged and does not focus the beam. The only dynamic-source run uses a rate
rescaled by 1000, and the steady state at the design pressure is bracketed analytically,
not simulated.

% =====================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

A compact beam-ionized gas cell upstream of the main solenoid can compensate a multi-mA,
30-keV proton beam locally, but only with electron confinement, and compensation in the cell
alone does not deliver the beam to the spiral inflector. The main results are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The achievable neutralization is set by electron confinement, not by the ionization
rate or the gas species. Freely escaping electrons limit the cell to $\eta\sim10^{-3}$. In
seeded PIC, $\Htwo$ reaches $\eta_{\mathrm{net}}=\numpicHtwoeta$ because its ions leave the
beam, whereas Kr stays near \numpicKreta{}--\numpicKretamax.
\item The cell solenoid and end plugs at least 10~mm wide give $\tau_c=\numstCWtauc~\mu$s and
$\eta_{\mathrm{net}}=\numstCWeta$ on the production grid; 5~mm plugs shorten $\tau_c$ and
triple the beam divergence. Test electrons in the same static trap survive
\numstCtwotend~$\mu$s, so the steady state lies between $\eta_{\mathrm{ss}}\approx
\numstCWetass$ and the well-limited value near 1.
\item 90\% transmission into the inflector acceptance needs $\eta_{\mathrm{down}}\approx
\numstCWtwoetaninety$--0.9 along the solenoid and quadrupoles. Residual gas at $\numpHtwo$~Torr
provides $\lesssim\numstCWthreeetasol$ there, so downstream compensation, not the cell, limits
the design.
\item Electrons do not follow strong bunches. Only the RF-averaged compensation applies,
$\Keff/K_0\approx1-\etaavg/B_f$ at the peak, and a sine-bunched beam from the baseline buncher
position transmits \numstBfiveGbasea{} of the DC accepted current. A gain over DC needs
late bunching or a sawtooth waveform (alternative-placement study).
\end{enumerate}
\pending{Final conclusions after the $\tau_c$ convergence study (task 123).}

\section{Reproducibility}
All analytical numbers and Figs.~\ref{fig:layout}--\ref{fig:peak} are generated by
\texttt{python scripts/make\_manuscript\_figures.py} from the module
\texttt{plasma\_column.design\_estimates} and the tabulated cross sections in the
project repository. The script records the repository commit and environment in
\texttt{paper/manuscript/manuscript\_numbers.json}. The PIC numbers, Table~\ref{tab:pic}
and Figs.~\ref{fig:pictime}--\ref{fig:picpressure} are generated by
\texttt{python scripts/make\_manuscript\_pic\_results.py} from the production matrix
\texttt{cases/production.yaml}. The script freezes the beam-core values, time series and
radial profiles in \texttt{paper/manuscript/pic\_data/} together with the run metadata,
and \texttt{--from\_frozen} rebuilds the figures and macros without the simulation output.
The confinement, transport and bunched-beam numbers and
Figs.~\ref{fig:confinement}--\ref{fig:gain} are generated in the same way by
\texttt{python scripts/make\_manuscript\_study\_results.py}, which freezes the study
summaries in \texttt{paper/manuscript/study\_data/}.
